messages.content: I want to frame the goal precisely: enable safe sim-to-real transfer for robotic peg insertion when changes in friction and clearance are indistinguishable before contact. What does that constraint mean for the task?

It means the system cannot count on pre-contact observations to tell it which friction–clearance combination it is facing. The goal is to transfer from simulation to the real insertion task while coping with that ambiguity and maintaining safety. It does not say that the conditions become identifiable after contact, only that they are indistinguishable before it.
So a plan that depends on knowing the friction and clearance in advance would not address this goal?

Right. If the plan requires that information before contact, it relies on a distinction the task says is unavailable at that point. The goal leaves open how the system might act under that uncertainty; it does not prescribe a particular method.
What is the insertion-performance target?

The target is at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations, using at most 20 real adaptation trials. “Held-out” matters: the success requirement concerns combinations outside those used to establish the approach, rather than only familiar combinations.
Are those 20 trials just a suggested amount of real-world practice?

No. “At most 20 real adaptation trials” is a limit in the stated requirement. The goal pairs that limit with the ≥90% insertion-success target; it does not permit an unspecified number of additional real adaptation trials to reach the target.
Does the wording say whether the 20-trial limit is counted separately for each held-out combination?

It does not specify that accounting detail. The stated constraint is at most 20 real adaptation trials. A more detailed evaluation protocol would have to make clear how the trial budget is counted; we should not assume a per-combination or pooled interpretation from this wording alone.
And what is the safety requirement while adapting?
Peak contact force must stay below 20 N during adaptation. The same below-20 N limit also applies during deployment, so safety is not only a condition on the adaptation trials.
Is reaching exactly 20 N within that limit?
No. The requirement says “below 20 N,” which is a strict threshold. It is different from saying “at or below 20 N.”
Could a high insertion-success rate compensate for exceeding the force limit occasionally?

Not under the stated goal. Insertion success and the peak-contact-force bound are separate requirements: the target calls for ≥90% success across the held-out combinations while keeping peak contact force below 20 N during adaptation and deployment.
What does “without privileged state observations” add?

The approach cannot depend on access to privileged observations of the underlying state. That restriction applies to meeting the goal, including the insertion-performance and force requirements. It is especially relevant to the pre-contact ambiguity: the task does not allow an unavailable state readout to stand in for information that ordinary pre-contact observations cannot distinguish.
Does that phrase rule out using any information obtained after contact?

The goal does not say that. It rules out privileged state observations, and it says friction and clearance changes are indistinguishable before contact. It does not specify which non-privileged observations, if any, are available after contact, or require a particular way of using them.
Is the objective to estimate friction and clearance accurately, then?

Not as stated. The objective is safe sim-to-real transfer for peg insertion under that ambiguity. Accurate estimation is not listed as a separate success criterion; the explicit criteria are insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations, the real-adaptation-trial limit, and the peak-contact-force bound without privileged state observations.
Can we say from the goal alone that those targets have been achieved?

No. It states what an approach needs to achieve, not an experimental result. We would need evidence before claiming ≥90% insertion success within at most 20 real adaptation trials or claiming that peak contact force remained below 20 N throughout adaptation and deployment.
What approach could address the pre-contact ambiguity in the peg-insertion goal?

One proposal is to use wrench-guided microdithers to infer beliefs about friction and clearance, then adapt impedance within 20 real trials using an 18 N predictive shield. It is a proposed approach, not a claim that the insertion-success or force targets have already been met.
Why put the microdithers before impedance adaptation?

The proposed order is to gather contact-related information through wrench-guided microdithers, form friction–clearance beliefs from it, and then use those beliefs while adapting impedance. That order responds to the fact that friction and clearance changes are indistinguishable before contact. It does not assume they can be identified in advance.
What does “wrench-guided” mean here?

In this context, a wrench is force-and-torque information. Calling the microdithers wrench-guided indicates that such information guides the small probing motions. The proposal does not specify a probing trajectory, sensor configuration, or inference algorithm.
Are the microdithers meant to reveal the exact friction and clearance values?

The proposal says to infer friction–clearance beliefs, not to recover exact values. A belief can represent uncertainty about the conditions, which matters when different friction–clearance possibilities are indistinguishable before contact. How precise those beliefs become is not established by the proposal.
So the system would probe rather than select an impedance setting solely from what it sees before contact?

That captures the proposed distinction. Wrench-guided microdithers are the information-gathering element, followed by impedance adaptation. The proposal does not spell out a rule for selecting settings, but it does not rely on pre-contact observations resolving the friction–clearance ambiguity.
What is being adapted when you say “impedance”?

Impedance refers broadly to how the robot responds mechanically to interaction, including its response to contact forces. The proposal is to adapt that behavior in light of the inferred friction–clearance beliefs. It does not specify which impedance parameters change, by how much, or according to what update rule.
And the adaptation still has the same real-world trial budget?

Yes. The proposal explicitly says to adapt impedance within 20 real trials. That aligns with the goal’s limit of at most 20 real adaptation trials; the proposal does not add permission for further real adaptation trials.
What role does the 18 N predictive shield play?

It is the proposed safety element accompanying impedance adaptation. The phrase “18 N predictive shield” identifies a predictive shield with an 18 N threshold, but does not specify its prediction model, intervention rule, or achieved force bound. Its intended role is to help manage contact-force risk while the robot adapts.
Is 18 N the same as the goal’s force limit?

No. The proposal names an 18 N predictive shield, while the goal requires peak contact force to stay below 20 N during adaptation and deployment. Those are different numbers with different roles: an element of the proposed approach versus the required limit on actual peak contact force.
Can I assume the shield guarantees that actual peak force will stay below 20 N?

No. The proposal alone does not establish a guarantee about actual peak force. Meeting the goal would require keeping peak contact force below 20 N in both adaptation and deployment, without privileged state observations; naming an 18 N predictive shield does not by itself demonstrate that outcome.
Does the proposal say the shield is only used during the 20 adaptation trials?

It says to adapt impedance within 20 real trials using an 18 N predictive shield. It does not explicitly specify the shield’s deployment-time use. Regardless, the underlying goal’s below-20 N peak-contact-force requirement applies during deployment as well as adaptation.
Would it be accurate to describe the approach as using the wrench signal to separate friction from clearance after contact?

That would be stronger than what is stated. The proposal is to use wrench-guided microdithers to infer friction–clearance beliefs. It does not promise that the two factors become separately identifiable, or specify how any ambiguity remaining after contact is resolved.
How does this connect to the held-out-combination performance target?

The proposal is intended to address the peg-insertion goal, including at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations. Belief inference and impedance adaptation describe a possible way to cope with differing conditions, but the proposal supplies no success measurements or evidence that it reaches ≥90% on held-out combinations.
Does using a wrench count as a privileged state observation?

Wrench information describes interaction forces and torques; it is not, by itself, a statement that the system has privileged access to the true friction or clearance state. The proposal calls for beliefs inferred from wrench-guided microdithers, not direct observation of the underlying friction–clearance values. Any implementation would still have to satisfy the goal’s restriction against privileged state observations.
Could I summarize the proposed sequence as contact-informed belief formation, followed by shielded impedance adaptation?

Yes, provided the specific terms remain clear: wrench-guided microdithers are proposed to infer friction–clearance beliefs, followed by impedance adaptation within 20 real trials using an 18 N predictive shield. The summary should not imply that the beliefs are exact, the shield guarantees the force limit, or the required success rate has already been achieved.
Can sub-18 N microdithers distinguish friction from clearance using wrist-wrench transients before the peg wedges?

That is an open question, not an established capability. It asks whether the changing wrist force-and-torque measurements produced during microdithers below 18 N contain enough information to tell a friction change from a clearance change before wedging occurs. The stated pre-contact ambiguity does not answer what can be distinguished once contact produces wrench information.
What exactly would count as distinguishing the two?

It would mean that the information available in those wrist-wrench transients supports telling whether a difference is attributable to friction or to clearance, rather than merely indicating that contact conditions differ. Forming a belief over possible friction–clearance conditions is weaker than reliably separating the two causes.
Why specify wrist-wrench transients instead of just the wrist wrench?

“Transients” focuses the question on how the measured forces and torques change over time during the microdithers, rather than on an isolated measurement. The question does not state that any particular transient pattern uniquely identifies friction or clearance; whether the changes carry discriminating information is precisely what remains open.
Is this asking for a distinction before contact?

No. The question concerns information from microdithers and wrist-wrench transients before the peg wedges. That is distinct from the goal’s statement that friction and clearance changes are indistinguishable before contact. “Before wedging” identifies the proposed window for making the distinction; it does not assert that a distinction is available before contact.
So the time window matters as much as the force level?

Both are explicit constraints on the question. It asks whether the distinction can be made using sub-18 N microdithers and using the resulting wrist-wrench transients before the peg wedges. An observation that only becomes informative after wedging would not answer that question as posed.
Does sub-18 N mean the force may reach 18 N?

Taken literally, “sub-18 N” means below 18 N, not equal to 18 N. The question does not specify a separate force value for any other part of the insertion, or establish that the overall peak contact force will satisfy the goal’s below-20 N limit.
Could the microdithers reveal that something changed without showing which of friction and clearance changed?

Yes, that is an important logical distinction. A transient might be informative about the presence of a difference without being sufficient to attribute it to friction rather than clearance. The question asks about that stronger, cause-specific distinction; it does not supply evidence that the distinction is possible.
Would a belief about friction and clearance answer the question automatically?

No. A belief can still leave both explanations plausible. To answer this question affirmatively, the wrist-wrench transients from sub-18 N microdithers would need to provide a meaningful way to distinguish friction from clearance before the peg wedges, not merely provide information that leaves the two confounded.
Is the question claiming that wedging actually happens during the microdithers?

No. “Before the peg wedges” sets a timing boundary for the proposed inference. It does not say that a peg necessarily wedges, that the microdithers cause wedging, or that a particular amount of time is available beforehand.
Can we infer from the wording that the wrist-wrench signals must have different signatures for friction and clearance?

We cannot infer that they do. The question is asking whether the transients can provide that distinction. It names the source of information and the constraints under which it would have to work, but it provides no observed signatures or demonstration of separability.
How does the 18 N figure here relate to the 18 N predictive shield in the proposed approach?

This question specifically describes microdithers as sub-18 N; the proposal separately names an 18 N predictive shield. The shared number does not establish that the shield enforces the microdither condition, or that either one guarantees the goal’s below-20 N peak contact force during adaptation and deployment.
If the distinction is possible only with privileged knowledge of the actual friction and clearance, would that answer the question?

No. The question asks whether wrist-wrench transients from the specified microdithers can distinguish the two. Access to the underlying values through privileged state observations would sidestep that information question and would not satisfy the broader goal’s restriction against privileged state observations.
And a promising transient alone would not establish the insertion target?

Correct. Distinguishing friction from clearance before wedging, if possible, would address an information question. It would not by itself establish ≥90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations within at most 20 real adaptation trials, or demonstrate peak contact force below 20 N during adaptation and deployment.

Here is the hypothesis I want to consider: under 18 N, two-axis microdithers reveal clearance-dependent deadbands and friction-dependent wrench hysteresis, enabling ≥85% held-out regime identification before wedging. How should I read it?

It proposes a specific answer to the information question: two-axis microdithers under 18 N might produce distinguishable wrist-wrench behavior before the peg wedges. The proposed cues are deadbands that depend on clearance and wrench hysteresis that depends on friction. The predicted outcome is at least 85% identification of held-out regimes before wedging. These are hypothesized effects and performance, not reported findings.
What does “two-axis” contribute to the claim?

It specifies that the microdithers involve two axes, rather than leaving the probing direction unspecified. The hypothesis does not name those axes or claim that any particular motion pattern has been shown to work. The two-axis condition is part of what would have to be true of the proposed information-gathering action.
Is “under 18 N” a strict limit here?

Yes. Read literally, it means below 18 N, not at or below 18 N. It constrains the microdithers in this hypothesis; the statement does not, by itself, establish a bound on every contact force throughout insertion.
Explain a clearance-dependent deadband without treating it as an observation we've already made.

A deadband, in general terms, is a range of small motion over which the measured response changes little or not at all. The hypothesis is that a feature of that kind in the response to two-axis microdithers depends on clearance. It does not provide a measured deadband, a formula for it, or evidence that clearance is its unique cause.
And what would “friction-dependent wrench hysteresis” mean?

Wrench hysteresis means that the force-and-torque response can depend on the path or direction of the motion, not just on a single instantaneous position. The hypothesis says that such a feature would depend on friction. It does not specify the shape or magnitude of the hysteresis, nor does it establish that any observed hysteresis must be due to friction.
Are those cues supposed to make friction and clearance completely separable?

The hypothesis predicts enough information for ≥85% held-out regime identification before wedging; it does not claim perfect separation. It also does not say the underlying friction and clearance values could be recovered exactly. The proposed relationship between each cue and each condition is a way the regimes might become distinguishable, subject to uncertainty and possible mistakes.
Could both factors still affect the same wrist-wrench transient?

The hypothesis does not rule that out. Calling one feature clearance-dependent and another friction-dependent does not assert that either feature is affected exclusively by one factor. The central question is whether the proposed features carry enough distinguishing information despite any ambiguity.
What is the significance of “before wedging” in this prediction?

It sets a deadline for identification. The predicted ≥85% held-out regime identification must be available before the peg wedges, rather than depending on information that appears only afterward. The hypothesis does not say that wedging necessarily occurs or specify how long that pre-wedging interval lasts.
Does “held-out regime identification” necessarily mean estimating numerical friction and clearance values?

No. The wording refers to identifying regimes, not to exact numerical estimation of both physical quantities. It also does not specify how regimes are defined or how held-out cases are selected. Those details should not be filled in as though they were part of the hypothesis.
Why state ≥85% rather than simply saying the cues are informative?

The ≥85% figure makes the prediction quantitative. It says the proposed cues should enable at least that level of held-out regime identification before wedging, which is stronger and more specific than merely suggesting that the signals may contain some information. It remains a predicted threshold, not an achieved result.
Would noticing a deadband and some hysteresis be enough to establish the full hypothesis?

No. The full hypothesis links the deadband to clearance, the wrench hysteresis to friction, and both to ≥85% held-out regime identification before wedging using two-axis microdithers under 18 N. Merely observing features that resemble a deadband and hysteresis would not, on its own, establish those dependencies or the identification prediction.
Can I phrase it as the robot already knows which regime it is in after the first dither?

That would go beyond the statement. The hypothesis does not say identification happens after a particular dither, that it is certain for any individual case, or that it has already occurred. It predicts a held-out identification level of ≥85% before wedging under the stated conditions.
Does this hypothesis require privileged access to the true friction and clearance during operation?

Not as written. Its proposed information comes from the wrench behavior associated with the microdithers, rather than from a direct readout of the underlying friction and clearance. The hypothesis does not specify every observation available to the robot, but it does not make privileged state observations part of the claimed cue.
Is the 85% figure an insertion-success prediction?

No. It is a prediction about held-out regime identification before wedging. Identifying a regime and completing a peg insertion are different outcomes; this hypothesis alone does not state an insertion-success result.
How certain should the wording sound if I restate the idea?

Keep it conditional: under 18 N, two-axis microdithers are hypothesized to reveal clearance-dependent deadbands and friction-dependent wrench hysteresis, enabling ≥85% held-out regime identification before the peg wedges. Avoid wording such as “have revealed” or “achieve” if it would present the prediction as an observed result.
And if the wrench changes during the two-axis motion, can I immediately assign one part of the change to clearance and another to friction?

No. The hypothesis proposes those dependencies, but an observed change by itself would not justify that assignment. What matters is whether the proposed deadband and hysteresis features actually distinguish the friction–clearance regimes to the predicted degree within the under-18 N, pre-wedging conditions.
How would we test the two-axis microdither hypothesis without treating its predicted identification rate as an established result?

The proposed activity is to test shielded two-axis microdithers on 36 held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs. For those tests, score pre-wedging identification accuracy from wrist-wrench traces and score peak force. That would evaluate the hypothesis; the activity description does not report any outcomes.
Why specify 36 pairs rather than just saying we will test in simulation?

Thirty-six is the stated number of held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs in this activity. It makes the scope of the proposed test specific. The description does not say how those pairs are selected or how many friction or clearance values they contain individually.
Does a pair mean one friction condition combined with one clearance condition?

Yes—that is the natural reading of a friction–clearance pair. The activity calls for 36 such pairs in simulation and says they are held out. It does not provide their numerical values or say that all possible combinations are included.
What exactly is being tested on those pairs?

The specified action is shielded two-axis microdithers. The resulting wrist-wrench traces are the stated basis for scoring identification before wedging, while peak force is also scored. The activity does not prescribe the microdither motions, shield mechanism, or identification procedure in further detail.
Does “shielded” mean we can assume the force stays under 18 N?

No. The hypothesis concerns microdithers under 18 N, and this activity calls for testing shielded microdithers and scoring peak force. The word “shielded” alone does not establish the peak force attained in the simulated tests; measuring or scoring peak force is part of finding out what happens.
If the shield has an 18 N threshold, could we just report that threshold as the peak force?

No. A threshold associated with a shield is not a measurement of the actual peak force. The activity specifically calls for scoring peak force, so the force outcome must be kept distinct from a stated or intended shield threshold.
Why use wrist-wrench traces for the identification score?

They are the proposed source of information about the friction–clearance condition during the microdithers. Scoring identification from those traces directly examines whether the contact-related signals contain useful distinguishing information. The activity does not assume that the traces will succeed in distinguishing the conditions.
What does “pre-wedging” change about the scoring?

It restricts the identification assessment to what is available before the peg wedges. A correct identification that relies on information appearing only after wedging would not demonstrate the pre-wedging identification described in the activity.
Are identification accuracy and peak force the same score here?

No. Identification accuracy concerns how often the friction–clearance regimes are identified correctly before wedging from wrist-wrench traces. Peak force concerns the largest contact force reached in the tests. The activity calls for assessing both, without supplying their values.
Would this activity directly test the hypothesis’s ≥85% held-out regime-identification prediction?

It is designed to evaluate that prediction: the pairs are held out, and identification accuracy is scored before wedging from wrist-wrench traces produced with two-axis microdithers. The hypothesis predicts ≥85% held-out regime identification under 18 N. The activity description, however, does not say what accuracy or peak force the tests produce.
Does scoring peak force matter even if the identification accuracy turns out to be high?

Yes. The hypothesis places the microdithers under 18 N, so force is relevant independently of identification accuracy. A high accuracy score by itself would not show that the stated force condition was met.
Can we call these 36 simulated tests the 20 real adaptation trials?

No. These are tests on 36 held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs. The goal’s limit of at most 20 real adaptation trials refers to real trials, not to the number of simulated pairs in this activity.
If this simulation activity goes well, would that alone prove the full peg-insertion goal?

No. This activity evaluates pre-wedging identification and peak force in simulated tests. It does not, by itself, establish ≥90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations within at most 20 real adaptation trials, or show that peak contact force stays below 20 N during real adaptation and deployment without privileged state observations.
Do we already have a result for any of the 36 held-out pairs?

No result is provided here. The node specifies an activity to test the shielded two-axis microdithers and score identification accuracy and peak force; it does not report measurements, successful identifications, or failures.
Could we say the activity establishes clearance-dependent deadbands and friction-dependent wrench hysteresis?

Not in advance. Those are proposed features in the hypothesis being evaluated. This activity specifies tests and scores, but provides neither wrist-wrench observations nor an analysis showing that particular features depend on clearance or friction.
What is the most precise one-sentence description of the activity?
Test shielded two-axis microdithers on 36 held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs, scoring pre-wedging identification accuracy from wrist-wrench traces and scoring peak force.
What did the tests on the held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs show?
Across 36 held-out simulated pairs, wrist-wrench microdithers identified 32 of 36 regimes before wedging. The highest contact force recorded across those tests was 17.2 N.
Is 32/36 an insertion-success count?
No. It counts regimes identified before wedging, not completed peg insertions. The evidence does not report insertion-success outcomes.
Can you express the identification count as a percentage?
32 divided by 36 is approximately 88.9%. That percentage describes pre-wedging regime identification across the 36 held-out simulated pairs; it is not an insertion-success rate.
Does the result tell us what happened in each of the other four pairs?
No. The aggregate count leaves four pairs outside the 32 identified regimes, but it does not say whether those cases were misidentified, left unidentified, or handled in some other way.
What is the scope of the 17.2 N number?

It is the highest contact force reported across the 36 held-out simulated pairs. It is not described as the force in every pair, an average force, or a prediction of what force would occur in a real trial.
Does this evidence show that the wrist-wrench traces contained a clearance-dependent deadband and friction-dependent hysteresis?

Those features are not reported in this evidence. It reports the aggregate pre-wedging identification count and the highest contact force, without describing the trace features responsible for individual identifications.
Can I conclude that friction and clearance were estimated as exact numerical values?
No. The reported outcome is identification of regimes. It gives no numerical friction or clearance estimates and no per-pair account of how the regimes were identified.
Does “before wedging” apply to all 32 identified regimes?
Yes. The evidence says the wrist-wrench microdithers identified 32 of the 36 regimes before wedging. It does not give a more specific identification time within that pre-wedging period.
Were these 36 real adaptation trials?
No. The 36 pairs were simulated and held out. This evidence reports simulation results, not outcomes from real adaptation trials.
Does the force figure establish what will happen during deployment?
No. The 17.2 N figure is an observed maximum across the reported simulated tests. It does not establish the peak contact force during real adaptation or deployment.
Could I report this as 36 successful identifications because all 36 pairs were tested?
No. Testing 36 pairs is different from identifying their regimes. The reported count is 32 identified regimes out of 36 held-out simulated pairs.
What's a concise way to state the evidence without extending its scope?
In tests across 36 held-out simulated friction–clearance pairs, wrist-wrench microdithers identified 32/36 regimes before wedging, and the highest contact force was 17.2 N.
What is the decision following the simulated tests?

Advance shielded microdithers to a 20-trial real pilot. The stated basis for that decision is that simulated identification reached 89%, with a peak contact force of 17.2 N. The pilot is a next step, not a completed real-world result.
Does the 89% figure describe what we expect the real pilot to achieve?
No. It describes identification in simulation. The decision does not state a predicted identification rate for the 20 real trials, and it does not report any real-pilot outcomes.
Is that identification rate the same as insertion success?

No. Regime identification and successful peg insertion are different outcomes. The 89% figure is simulated identification, not the goal’s ≥90% insertion-success measure across held-out friction–clearance combinations.
How should I describe the 17.2 N figure?
As the peak contact force reported for the simulated tests cited in the decision. It is below 20 N, but it does not establish what peak force will be in the real pilot or during deployment.
Why mention both numbers when stating the decision?

They convey two distinct aspects of the cited simulation result: 89% concerns identification, while 17.2 N concerns peak contact force. Both are part of the stated rationale for advancing the shielded microdithers, without turning either simulated result into a claim about real-world performance.
Does “advance” mean the 20 real trials have already happened?
No. It means moving the shielded microdithers forward to a 20-trial real pilot. Nothing in this decision reports completed pilot trials or their results.
Can I call it an unrestricted real-world rollout?
No. The decision specifies a 20-trial real pilot, not unrestricted deployment. It does not say what happens after the pilot.
Does the decision specify how the 20 pilot trials are divided among friction–clearance conditions?
No. It specifies the pilot size but not the conditions assigned to individual trials or how they are distributed. Those details should not be presented as part of this decision.
Does using shielded microdithers in the pilot guarantee that contact force will stay below 20 N?

No guarantee is stated. The 17.2 N peak was observed in simulation. The goal still requires peak contact force below 20 N during real adaptation and deployment, without privileged state observations; the decision to run a shielded pilot does not establish that those conditions have been met.
Could the simulated identification number alone establish that the sim-to-real goal has been reached?

No. The decision is to proceed to real trials on the basis of simulated identification and force results. It does not establish real-world insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations, completion within the real adaptation-trial limit, or the required force bound during real adaptation and deployment.
What's the most faithful brief statement of the decision?
Advance shielded microdithers to a 20-trial real pilot, citing 89% simulated identification and a 17.2 N simulated peak contact force.
What is the plan for the real pilot?

Pilot shielded, wrench-conditioned impedance for 20 real adaptation trials. Then evaluate held-out peg insertions for at least 90% success and peak contact forces below 20 N. This is a plan and an evaluation target, not a report that either threshold has been met.
What does “wrench-conditioned impedance” mean in this plan?

It means the impedance behavior is to be conditioned on wrench information—force-and-torque information from interaction. The plan does not specify which impedance parameters change, how wrench information affects them, or the update rule.
And what does “shielded” establish?

It identifies a safety component of the planned pilot. It does not, by itself, establish that actual contact-force peaks will remain below 20 N. Those peaks are an outcome the plan calls for evaluating.
Are the 20 trials simulated or real?
Real. The plan specifies 20 real adaptation trials for the pilot. It does not report results from those trials.
Is 20 an upper limit here, or a count the pilot is planned to run?

The pilot is described as having 20 real adaptation trials. That fits within the broader goal’s limit of at most 20 real adaptation trials. The plan does not describe additional real adaptation trials beyond those 20.
Does the plan say how those trials are allocated among friction–clearance conditions?
No. It does not specify the conditions used in individual adaptation trials, their order, or how trials are allocated. The stated count is 20 real adaptation trials.
What is evaluated after adaptation?

Held-out insertions are evaluated for two outcomes: insertion success of at least 90% and peak contact force below 20 N. The plan does not specify the number of held-out insertions or the detailed evaluation protocol.
Can we assume the held-out insertions are part of the 20 adaptation trials?

The wording distinguishes the 20 real adaptation trials from the evaluation of held-out insertions, but it does not explain how evaluation trials are counted or scheduled. We should not assume an accounting rule that the plan does not state.
Why evaluate held-out insertions rather than only the adaptation trials?

The performance target concerns insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations. Evaluating held-out insertions asks whether the approach works beyond the conditions encountered in adaptation, rather than judging it solely by what happens during adaptation. The plan does not specify how the held-out combinations are selected.
Is the ≥90% figure for identifying the friction–clearance regime?
No. In this plan, ≥90% is the target for successful held-out insertions. Identifying a regime and completing an insertion are different outcomes.
How strict is the force target?

It is strict: “<20 N peaks” means peak contact force below 20 N, not equal to 20 N. The broader goal applies that bound during adaptation and deployment. This plan calls for evaluating peaks in the held-out insertions as well; it does not report measured forces.
Would meeting the success target excuse a peak of 20 N?
No. The plan asks for both ≥90% insertion success and peaks below 20 N. A peak of exactly 20 N would not satisfy the stated force threshold, regardless of the success rate.
Does the plan say the wrench signal gives direct access to the true friction and clearance?

No. Conditioning impedance on wrench information is not the same as observing the underlying friction and clearance directly. The plan does not introduce privileged state observations; the broader goal requires meeting its targets without them.
Does this plan include an unrestricted deployment phase?

It specifies a real adaptation pilot and evaluation of held-out insertions, not an unrestricted deployment phase. The goal’s below-20 N force requirement also applies during deployment, but this plan does not state deployment outcomes or a deployment procedure.
What can we conclude right now about real-world success and force?

Only what will be tested: shielded, wrench-conditioned impedance is planned for 20 real adaptation trials, followed by evaluation of held-out insertions against ≥90% success and <20 N peak contact force. The plan provides no real-pilot measurements or held-out insertion results.
What activity is specified for the pilot?

Run 20 shielded real adaptation trials, then test 60 held-out insertions across 12 friction–clearance pairs, logging insertion success and peak force. This describes the activity and what to record; it does not report the results.
Which number refers to adaptation and which refers to evaluation?

The 20 trials are the shielded real adaptation trials. The 60 are held-out insertion tests, conducted across 12 friction–clearance pairs. The activity treats adaptation trials and held-out insertion tests as distinct parts of the work.
Does this say that each of the 12 pairs gets five insertion tests?
No. Sixty divided by twelve is five, but the activity does not specify an equal allocation. It states only the total of 60 held-out insertions and that they span 12 friction–clearance pairs.
What does a friction–clearance pair represent here?

It is a combination of a friction condition and a clearance condition. The activity specifies 12 such pairs for the held-out insertion tests, without giving their values or describing how they were selected.
Does “held-out” apply to the adaptation trials too?
The wording explicitly calls the 60 insertions held out. It does not label the 20 real adaptation trials as held out or specify the relationship between their conditions and the 12 evaluation pairs.
What measurements are we logging?

Insertion success and peak force are the specified logged outcomes for the held-out tests. Success records whether an insertion succeeds; peak force records the highest contact force reached. No values for either outcome are given here.
